summary: Catalogs known problems with web caching proxies and cache servers, with discussion and workarounds. The aim is to improve conditions by describing the problems.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a list of ways the web's helper copy-machines go wrong, and how to fix them.

subtitle: A catalog of problems with web caching proxies and proposed solutions.

tldr.problem: Web caching proxies are widely deployed to improve performance, but they have numerous known problems that can cause data inconsistency, performance degradation, and operational complexity.
tldr.mechanism: The document catalogs these problems systematically, grouping them by type (specification, architectural, and implementation issues), and provides discussion of workarounds and potential solutions for each.
tldr.outcome: By documenting these issues openly, the document aims to encourage the web caching community to address problems and improve interoperability.

today: RFC 3143 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a reference document for understanding persistent issues in HTTP caching infrastructure, although modern HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 protocols have evolved to address some of these concerns.

sections.title: Introduction to Proxy Problems
sections.content:
Web caching proxies are intermediaries that sit between clients and origin servers, storing copies of content to improve performance and reduce network load. However, these systems have accumulated a number of known problems that can cause failure modes ranging from subtle data inconsistency to dramatic performance degradation.

This document catalogs these problems systematically. It organizes issues into three main categories: specification problems where the HTTP/1.1 standard itself is ambiguous or incomplete; architectural problems inherent to how proxies are deployed and how they relate to clients and servers; and implementation problems where vendors have not correctly followed the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Web helper machines are supposed to make the internet faster by keeping copies of stuff. But they get confused about when things change, and they break in lots of different ways.

sections.title: How Proxies Work and What Goes Wrong
sections.content:
Proxies operate as application-level intermediaries that intercept HTTP requests from clients and either serve cached responses or forward requests to origin servers. Some proxies are explicit, configured by the user agent, while others use interception (also called transparent proxies) where clients are unaware they are sending traffic through a proxy.

A key challenge is that proxies must make caching decisions with incomplete information. The HTTP/1.1 specification defines headers like Cache-Control and Vary to help proxies understand when cached responses are safe to reuse, but these mechanisms have gaps. The Vary header, for example, is meant to handle content negotiation but becomes problematic when new HTTP extensions are introduced that older proxies don't understand. Proxies may cache a response that is inappropriate for a later client that doesn't understand the same extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy has to guess whether saved content is still good for the next person who asks. The instructions in HTTP are confusing and incomplete, so the proxy often makes the wrong choice.

sections.title: Specification and Architectural Problems
sections.content:
The specification problems identified include the underspecified Vary header and the loss of valuable metadata when HTTP/1.1 proxies forward requests from HTTP/1.0 clients. The Vary header problem is particularly subtle: proxies cannot safely cache responses when the server uses unknown protocol extensions, even if the Vary header is present, because older proxies lack the knowledge to understand what the extension does.

Architectural problems stem from two primary deployment scenarios. Explicit proxies require configuration by users and can be bypassed, while interception proxies operate transparently but break important client behaviors. Interception proxies prevent clients from sending cache-control directives like no-cache, because clients believe they are connected directly to the origin server and expect such directives to affect the server's behavior, not a proxy's. Interception proxies also block new HTTP methods, since any unknown method triggers a 501 error response.

Other architectural problems arise from proxy meshes, where caching proxies peer with each other to share content. These mesh arrangements can break HTTP's serialization guarantees: a client might receive stale content from a different path through the mesh than they received fresher content from earlier.
sections.plainLanguage: The instructions in HTTP are incomplete when new features get added. Proxy networks also get tangled together, and you might get old stuff from one path and new stuff from another path.

sections.title: Implementation Problems and Real-World Issues
sections.content:
Implementation problems include incorrect handling of Cache-Control headers, lack of compliance with HTTP/1.1, poor support for ETags, and servers that send incorrect Content-Length headers. User agent failover between proxies is also erratic, with no standard behavior defined. When a browser detects that its primary proxy is down, it may wait arbitrary lengths of time before trying an alternative proxy, creating confusion for end users.

Peer selection in proxy meshes using the Internet Cache Protocol (ICP) is inefficient in networks with heterogeneous latency and bandwidth. ICP selects peers based on which responds first, not on which can deliver content fastest. Additionally, ICP exhibits O(n²) scaling properties, where peering with many other proxies creates an explosion of ICP traffic that can dominate HTTP traffic within a network.
sections.plainLanguage: Proxy software often doesn't follow the rules correctly. Proxy networks are also slow at picking which other proxy to ask, and sometimes all the asking uses up more bandwidth than the actual content.

sections.title: Solutions and Workarounds
sections.content:
For specification problems, solutions include modifying the HTTP/1.1 specification to prohibit caching of responses with unknown status codes, or having proxy implementers treat the presence of a Vary header as an implicit no-store directive except for known status codes. Designers of HTTP extensions should consider mechanisms other than Vary to prevent incorrect caching.

For architectural problems, the most direct solution is to eliminate the need for interception proxies by having all proxies be explicitly configured. This restores proper context awareness to the client. For proxy mesh performance, the use of cache digest protocols or proxy clustering approaches can replace ICP. For poor convergence in multi-homed environments, the solution is to design proxy hierarchies without high-latency variance among sibling peers.
sections.plainLanguage: Use explicit proxies instead of hidden ones, so clients know where they are. Replace slow mesh protocols with better ones. Follow the rules more carefully.
